# Error tracking — wiring the launch gate

**Status:** Active — **E1a, E1b, E2a and E2b all landed (2026-09-13 → 09-17); E3 (sourcemaps + releases) is the last chunk.** Until it lands every browser stack trace Sentry shows is minified, so the web half reports but is not yet readable. The api reports, scrubbed, and is inert until `SENTRY_DSN` is set, so the account can arrive later without touching code. The gate itself is [observability-floor.md § Chunk 2](observability-floor.md); this note is its analysis and plan. The decision it was waiting on is made here: **hosted Sentry at launch, self-hosting deferred and cheap to revisit.** The work is five chunks and needs no box. Nothing about it is novel except the redaction problem, which is the one part that can make this change *worse* than shipping without it — read that section before writing any code.

## The decision

**Hosted Sentry free tier.** Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. **It survives the thing it monitors.** A tracker on the same VPS cannot report that the VPS is gone, and that is the failure it most needs to report. Single-box deployments have no second box to fall back to.
2. **It costs no memory.** The box is 8 GB ([hosting.md § Sizing implications](hosting.md#sizing-implications)), budgeted for vyoh plus about one more tenant, which only sharpens this. Sentry self-hosted wants roughly the whole box; GlitchTip or Bugsink want a few hundred MB and a database, which fits but is not free.
3. **The free tier is far past this app's volume.** A single-owner dashboard with a handful of visitors does not generate thousands of distinct errors a month. If it does, that is the signal, not the cost problem.

**What would change it:** a real need to keep error payloads on infrastructure we own — which for a public portfolio dashboard with no third-party user data is hard to argue — or blowing the free tier persistently.

**Why this is a cheap decision to get wrong.** Instrumentation targets Sentry's *protocol*, not its hosting. GlitchTip and Bugsink both speak it, so moving later is a DSN change and a redeploy, not re-instrumentation. That is the reason not to agonise here, and the reason self-hosting is a legitimate later move rather than a road not taken. GlitchTip would slot into the one-cluster-database-per-project convention already described in [hosting.md § Per-component conventions](hosting.md).

**Rejected: self-hosting Sentry itself.** Not a close call — its stack is sized for organisations, and running it beside the app it watches fails reason 1 anyway.

## Where it hooks — seven points, all of which already exist

On the request and cron paths, every exception is already caught; those catch sites simply have nowhere to send anything. That makes this a wiring job rather than a refactor, and it keeps the instrumentation small enough to review. It is **not** true that the processes are fully guarded: no `unhandledRejection` or `uncaughtException` handler exists anywhere in `apps/`, so a stray rejection off those paths still dies silently. Both SDKs install their own, which is a real side benefit of doing this at all.

**api**

- **[fallback-exception.filter.ts](../../../apps/api/src/fallback-exception.filter.ts)** is `@Catch()` and classifies every failure into a `Verdict`. Its `verdict.log` field is *deliberately undefined for a deliberate 4xx* — the comment there says those "are the handler's own answer and logging them would only bury the real failures". **That field is the report signal, but the level is not the predicate.** Read `classify()` before wiring: 5xx `HttpException`, `SteamRateLimiterTimeoutError` and every `SteamClientError` 429/502/504 all log at **`warn`**; only Prisma errors and the unknown catch-all reach `error`. So `level === "error"` would drop every upstream 5xx — including the Steam failure this note asks you to verify with. **Report where `verdict.log` is present and `verdict.status >= 500`**, which reports real failures and still never reports a 404 or a validation rejection. Getting this backwards is how a tracker becomes noise that nobody reads within a week.
- **[riot.exception-filter.ts](../../../apps/api/src/riot/riot.exception-filter.ts)** is `@Catch(RiotError)` and is registered *after* the catch-all, so Nest gives it every `RiotError` and the fallback filter never sees one. Missing this was a real gap found in review: it maps to 502/503/504 and logs at `warn`, so the entire LoL half of the app would have reported request failures nowhere while Steam's were tracked. Same predicate, 5xx only, so a 404 summoner miss and a Riot 429 stay out.
- **[sync-job-registry.service.ts](../../../apps/api/src/sync-jobs/sync-job-registry.service.ts)** already catches every cron failure, logs the stack, and stores a redacted one-liner for `/status`. Its `catch` is where a *background* failure should report, and it is the more valuable of the two: a cron that has been failing for a week is exactly the thing nobody notices, and `/status` shows only the latest run.

**web**

- **[error-boundary.tsx](../../../apps/web/src/components/error-boundary.tsx)** already exposes `onError?: (error: Error, info: ErrorInfo) => void`, invoked from `componentDidCatch`. Every boundary in the app routes through this one component, so a single default here covers the whole tree. Note [__root.tsx](../../../apps/web/src/routes/__root.tsx) already passes its own `onError` to play a sound — the reporting hook must compose with that rather than replace it.
- **`defaultErrorComponent` / `errorComponent`** in [router.tsx](../../../apps/web/src/router.tsx) and `__root.tsx` catch route-tier failures, which bypass the React boundary.
- **[node-adapter.ts](../../../apps/web/server/node-adapter.ts)** wraps every request in a `.catch()` that `console.error`s and writes a 500. This is where **SSR render failures** surface — they never reach a React boundary, because on the server there is no mounted tree left to catch them — and it is the natural `@sentry/node` init site for the web tier.
- **`QueryCache` / `MutationCache` `onError`** in `router.tsx`. Read the guard before touching it: the query handler splits on `query.state.data`. A **background refresh** failure (data present) toasts and is never reported — it is frequently just a flaky upstream, and the most likely source of quota burn in the whole app. A **first-load** failure (no data) does not toast, and reports at `query` tier only when the api cannot have seen it; see the E2b chunk below for why and for what dedupe does to the tier. `MutationCache.onError` has **no such guard** and fires on every mutation failure; those are owner-initiated writes and are worth reporting, so do not treat the two handlers as one decision.

## The redaction problem — read before writing code

This is the part that can make the change a regression. [F-5 in api-exposure-audit.md](api-exposure-audit.md) was the Steam Web API key being written to our own logs in cleartext on any fetch failure, because Steam passes its key as a query parameter. It was fixed 2026-08-03. **Sending error payloads to a third party re-opens exactly that surface, one layer out.**

The defence used to be `redactSecrets()` private to the sync-job registry, and it was **necessary but not sufficient**: it scrubs secret-looking **query parameters in a message string**, while a Sentry event is much wider — breadcrumbs including outbound HTTP URLs, request headers, stack-frame locals, and anything attached as `extra` or tags. Two gaps followed from that. *Reach*: the helper only ever saw one string. *Shape*: a header carries its credential as the whole value under a telling key, which no query-parameter pattern matches.

**E1a closed both** in [redaction.ts](../../../packages/shared/src/redaction.ts). `redactSecretsDeep` walks JSON-shaped data, and `isSecretKey` replaces a value outright when its key looks like a credential. Six properties are load-bearing and each is pinned by a test. Three of them were leaks found in review rather than foresight, which is the honest reason this section is long:

1. The cycle guard is scoped to the **current path**, not the whole walk. A guard that remembered every object would hand back the second occurrence of a shared reference unscrubbed, and a Sentry event routinely attaches one object at two points.
2. That path scoping costs breadth: a shared-reference graph is walked once per distinct path and multiplies out, so a **visit budget** bounds total work. It must be charged **per property and per array element**, not per object — charging per object still lets one visit build an output of unbounded width, which took 2 GB and died in exactly the shape the budget was added to prevent. Truncation writes the marker so a short object and an exhausted one are distinguishable.
3. A subtree past the depth cap, a cycle, and an exhausted budget all collapse to the marker rather than passing through unscanned.
4. **The key pattern must stay wide enough for `vyoh_session`.** Bounding a bare `session` to spare this app's play-session fields is right, but narrowing it to `session(id|key|token)` drops the owner's own login cookie, which is account takeover rather than lost context. `cookies?` is anchored plural so the whole bag goes regardless of the names inside it.
5. Nothing escapes, and a failure stays local. A throwing getter or a proxy trap that throws from `ownKeys` collapses **that value** to the marker; without containment at each level the outer guard replaces the entire event, so one hostile field would cost the whole report.
6. **The query pattern must not require a leading `?`.** Sentry stores `request.query_string` with it already stripped, so demanding one leaves the *first* parameter unscrubbed — frequently the key itself, which is F-5 over again one layer out. The same names arrive as **object keys** once parsed, which is why bare `key` and `code` are anchored matches in the key pattern, matching Steam's Web API key and GitHub's OAuth authorization code.

**Two costs paid deliberately.** Matching a bare `code` key redacts `err.code`, which is the primary Node and Prisma diagnostic (`ECONNREFUSED`, `P2002`) and is what the fallback filter branches on. That is a real loss, accepted because narrowing it back is how GitHub's OAuth authorization code leaks, and a missing error code is cheaper than a live credential. Separately, `redactSecretsDeep` returns the bare marker when a value defeats it, so **E1b's `beforeSend` must handle a string where the SDK expects an event or `null`** rather than passing it straight back.

**One deliberate passthrough, stated so it is not mistaken for an oversight:** a value that is neither string, array nor plain object — a Date, a class instance, an `Error` — passes through intact rather than being mangled into something it is not. That is safe for `beforeSend`, which receives an event an SDK has already normalised to plain JSON. It is *not* safe for un-normalised input, so do not hand it any. Where it cannot vouch for a value it substitutes the marker — losing context in a report is recoverable, leaking a credential is not.

**How to apply:** pass the whole event through `redactSecretsDeep` from `beforeSend`, `beforeSendTransaction` and the breadcrumb hook — every path out, not just `event.message`. Set `sendDefaultPii: false` explicitly rather than relying on the default. Then **verify by triggering a real Steam failure and reading the event in the Sentry UI**, not by reading the code — this is the one requirement in this note that a test cannot honestly close, because the thing being checked is what left the process.

## Sourcemaps

Recorded in [frontend-2026-gaps.md:501](../cross-cutting/frontend-2026-gaps.md): no sourcemap or upload pipeline exists. Confirmed 2026-09-13 — [vite.config.ts](../../../apps/web/vite.config.ts) sets `build.target` and `build.manifest` and no `build.sourcemap`, so the Vite production default of `false` applies. The `sourceMap: true` further up that file belongs to a Lightning CSS `transformCss` call and is a different API entirely. **Without this, every web stack trace Sentry shows is minified and useless**, which quietly makes the whole web half of this work worthless while appearing to succeed.

The usual objection to shipping sourcemaps is that they expose your source. **That objection does not apply here: the repo is public.** There is nothing to protect, so the simple path is available — generate them and let them be resolvable — rather than the upload-then-delete dance a closed-source project needs. Prefer Sentry's Vite plugin so releases are tagged and traces resolve without a fetch round-trip, but the fallback of simply serving them is acceptable and is not a security finding in this repo.

## Noise to filter before the first deploy

A tracker that cries wolf is worse than none, and each of these is known in advance:

- **TanStack SSR aborts.** "render was aborted by the server" fires whenever a client disconnects mid-render. Upstream noise, not a bug, and on a public site it happens constantly. Drop it in `beforeSend`.
- **ResizeObserver loop notices.** ✅ Filtered 2026-09-21, after one reached production from `/` on the day the browser tier started reporting. "ResizeObserver loop completed with undelivered notifications" is the spec's own bail-out — a callback resized something inside the tree it observes, so the browser delivers one more round and reports the remainder. It arrives as an `ErrorEvent` with no error object, no stack and `:0:0` for a location, which is how the issue was traced to the pre-init buffer's message synthesis rather than to the SDK's own handler. `BENIGN_ERROR_PATTERNS` in [early-errors.ts](../../../apps/web/src/lib/early-errors.ts) drops it at the buffer and feeds `ignoreErrors` in [instrument.ts](../../../apps/web/src/instrument.ts). Both ends, because the buffer holds ten events: a burst during hydration would evict the crash it exists to catch, which is the failure mode worth more than the noise.
- **Prefetch traffic.** [speculation-rules-prefetch.md:32](../cross-cutting/speculation-rules-prefetch.md) already sets the constraint that prefetch requests must not pollute error-tracking attributes.
- **Background query refresh failures**, per the `QueryCache` note above.
- **Known gap, accepted for now:** a Steam 429 reports nowhere. The catch-all filter excludes it by design and the awaited refresh path captures nothing, so upstream quota exhaustion is invisible. That is the one failure the `/status` board does surface, which is why it is a gap rather than a blocker.
- **Quota guard.** Set a sample rate before the first deploy, not after. Do not lean on deduplication for this: `dedupeIntegration` is not among the Node SDK's defaults, so nothing is collapsing repeats unless it is added explicitly. A crash loop can burn a month of free tier in minutes, and the deploy that causes it is exactly when the tracker must still be working.

## Chunks

Each is independently committable and needs no VPS.

- **E1a — scrubbing groundwork.** ✅ Shipped 2026-09-13. Needs no account. `redactSecrets`, `isSecretKey` and `redactSecretsDeep` in [redaction.ts](../../../packages/shared/src/redaction.ts), exported from the barrel, with `sync-job-registry.service.ts` switched off its private copy. The deep walker answers the reach problem above: it scans strings anywhere in a JSON-shaped event, and replaces a value outright when its *key* looks like a credential, which is what covers `request.headers`. Bounded depth and a cycle guard because it runs inside the error path and must not throw or hang. Values that are not strings, arrays or plain objects pass through rather than being half-rebuilt.
- **E1b — api wiring.** ✅ Shipped 2026-09-14, and it needed no account after all. `@sentry/nestjs` pinned at 10.73.0 (14 days' soak; npq's typosquat flag against `@sentry/nextjs` is a false positive, both are official packages in the same scope), [instrument.ts](../../../apps/api/src/instrument.ts) imported second in `main.ts` behind `dotenv/config` only, and `captureException` at the two hook points. **An absent DSN disables the SDK**, which is what let the wiring ship ahead of the account: switching reporting on is a config change, and every test and local run stays silent without special-casing.

  The report predicate is `verdict.log` present **and** `verdict.status >= 500`. A test pins a 503, which logs at `warn`, precisely because a level-based predicate would have reported none of the upstream failures. Two more pin that P2002 and P2025 stay out — the filter answers those as 409 and 404, and a constraint hit is the handler's answer rather than a fault. Reporting sits in `SyncJobRegistry.run()` only, and `execute()` deliberately does not report because it rethrows to its caller. Note the practical shape: `trigger()` routes through `run()`, so the only caller that reaches a controller — and therefore the filter — is the awaited `execute()` path. Tests pin both halves.

  **Verified against a local envelope receiver rather than by reading code**, per the requirement above: a DSN pointed at `127.0.0.1`, one `captureException` carrying a Steam key in the message, a bearer token under `authorization` and a session cookie, and the envelope read back. All three absent, `steamid=7` still present.

  **Worth knowing before E2:** Sentry attaches `pre_context` / `post_context`, the real source lines around each stack frame. The first run of that check reported two leaks that turned out to be the *probe script's own source* being shipped, because it hardcoded the fake secrets as literals. Harmless here, since the repo is public and holds no literal credentials. Be precise about why, because the loose version misleads: those lines **are** in the event by the time `beforeSend` runs, so the scrubber does see them. It simply cannot match them — source text spells a credential as `authorization: "Bearer …"`, which is neither a query parameter nor an object key. Source is therefore a surface the scrubber cannot defend, with its own rule: no literal secrets in committed code.

**Two more things the same review corrected**, both worth not re-deriving. `tracesSampleRate: 0` does *not* disable performance monitoring — the SDK gates on `!= null`, so a zero still installs the Express, Prisma, pg and http instrumentation plus OpenTelemetry and builds a span per request before discarding it. Omitting the key is what actually means no tracing. And `SENTRY_SAMPLE_RATE=` set-but-empty yields `Number("") === 0`, which the SDK accepts as valid and then drops every error while still looking enabled, so the fallback is `|| 1` rather than `??`.
- **E2a — SSR tier.** ✅ Shipped 2026-09-14. `@sentry/node` at 10.73.0 in `apps/web`, [server/instrument.ts](../../../apps/web/server/instrument.ts) imported first in `server/index.ts`, and `captureException` in the [node-adapter](../../../apps/web/server/node-adapter.ts) request catch — the only place an SSR render failure surfaces, since there is no mounted React tree left for a boundary to catch.

  **The SDK decision, checked rather than assumed.** `@sentry/tanstackstart-react` now carries a stable `latest` dist-tag versioned in lockstep with the rest of Sentry 10.x, which looks settled — but its README still opens "Official Sentry SDK for TanStack Start React (Beta)" and says so in bold. Taking the hand-wired `@sentry/node` path instead, because with tracing omitted the Start SDK's main value-add is router instrumentation we do not use, so the beta buys nothing here. Revisit for E2b only if the client side turns out to need it.

  **The client-disconnect filter landed with it**, in `beforeSend` rather than at the capture site, because the same error can arrive by paths that never reach the adapter's catch. The predicate lives in its own [client-disconnect.ts](../../../apps/web/server/client-disconnect.ts) so a test can reach it without importing a module whose whole purpose is `Sentry.init` — the Node SDK installs global handlers on init, which is not something a test suite should inherit.

  **`scrub` moved to `packages/shared` as `scrubPayload`** in the same change: the api had it privately, the web tier is the second consumer, and the cross-package rule in [repo-conventions.md](../../repo-conventions.md) makes consolidation a requirement rather than a preference at that point.

  **That import nearly shipped a boot loop, and the reason generalises.** `server/*.ts` runs as raw TypeScript under Node's type stripping, and **Node refuses to strip types from any file whose realpath sits under `node_modules`**. The web image builds with `pnpm deploy --prod`, which materialises workspace packages *inside* `node_modules`, so the first `import … from "@vyoh/shared"` would have killed the container on startup. The dev tree hides this completely: there `node_modules/@vyoh/shared` is a symlink whose realpath is `packages/shared`, outside `node_modules`, so running the entry locally succeeds and proves nothing. The api image already solves it by copying raw source beside a symlinked `node_modules`, and the web image now does the same. **Verified in the built container both ways**: booting the image logs `web listening` and reports healthy, while replacing the symlink with a real copy inside `node_modules` fails with `ERR_UNSUPPORTED_NODE_MODULES_TYPE_STRIPPING`. This is a container-divergence rule rather than a Sentry one, and probably belongs in [repo-conventions-web.md](../../repo-conventions-web.md) alongside the others.
- **E2b — browser.** Split in two once the bundle cost was measured. **Chunk 1 shipped 2026-09-17**: `@sentry/react` at 10.73.0, [src/instrument.ts](../../../apps/web/src/instrument.ts) scrubbing all three hooks, and the build plumbing that carries `VITE_SENTRY_DSN` / `VITE_SENTRY_SAMPLE_RATE`. **Chunk 2 shipped 2026-09-17** — the hook points.

  Reporting goes through [lib/report-error.ts](../../../apps/web/src/lib/report-error.ts), and the indirection is the load-bearing part: every caller sits in the initial bundle, so a static `@sentry/react` import from a boundary or from `router.tsx` would pull the SDK back over the budget chunk 1 measured. It `import()`s the instrument chunk instead, which `client.tsx` has already started, so the module cache serves it and a report raised before it lands waits rather than being dropped. `import.meta.env.SSR` compiles the whole path out of the server bundle, where `@sentry/node` is the right SDK.

  `ErrorBoundary` reports from `componentDidCatch` **before** calling the caller's `onError`, so the root boundary's sound cannot swallow a report by throwing. A **required** `tier` prop tags every event — `app-root`, `page`, `widget`, `route`, `mutation` — because severity differs by an order of magnitude across them and an untiered issue list cannot tell a degenerate chart from an outage. Required rather than defaulted for the same reason: every boundary routes through this one component, so a default would file a root-level failure under whatever the common case happened to be. `RouteErrorFallback` reports from an effect keyed on the error, since it also renders on the server and a retry re-renders it.

  **The two cache handlers are deliberately different decisions**, as the hook list above insists. `MutationCache` reports: a failed mutation is an owner-initiated write that did not happen, low volume by construction, and silence means the owner believes they changed something they did not. `QueryCache` does **not**, for the refresh case: a refresh of data already on screen fails mostly on a briefly flaky upstream, already toasts, and when the cause is a real 5xx the api reports it with better context, so reporting here duplicates that signal and is the largest quota risk in the app.

  **But read the guard before trusting that sentence — it is narrower than "background refresh".** `query.state.data === undefined` drops *every* failure with no cached data, and two of those reach nobody at all. A prime routed through [`primeQuietly`](../../../apps/web/src/lib/prime-quietly.ts) cannot escalate to an `errorComponent`, because its `allSettled` is precisely what stops the loader rejecting — eight route files rely on that. And a `useQuery` that no loader primes has no loader to reject either. Both failed silently: no toast, no report. **Closed 2026-09-25 by reporting that branch selectively, not by lifting the guard.** A first-load failure reports at a `query` tier unless it is an `HttpError` — the api answered, so a 5xx is already reported server-side and a 4xx was meant — or the visitor is offline. What that leaves is the class only the browser can see: an api it could not reach, a body that would not parse, a throw in the query function. A blocking prime's failure also reaches its `errorComponent`, which reports the same error object at `route` tier. `@sentry/browser`'s default `dedupeIntegration` — a default there, unlike the Node SDK — drops the repeat, but it keeps the **first** event, and `QueryCache.onError` runs before the rejection reaches the loader, so such a failure is usually filed under `query` rather than `route`. It also compares against the immediately previous event only, so a sibling failure in between lets both through. Seven fetchers threw a plain `Error` on a non-2xx and would have reported the api's own answers; they throw `HttpError` now, which also puts their 4xx under the no-retry rule. An edge 429 reaches the browser as a network error, since nginx's own answers carry no CORS header, so it reports once its retries run out. The Steam-429 gap stays open.

  **The SDK is a lazy chunk, and that was measured rather than assumed.** Statically imported it put the initial JS at 278.83 kB against a 255 kB budget. Dropping every default integration changed nothing (278.85) — the cost is the core client, not the integrations — and the `__SENTRY_TRACING__` / `__SENTRY_DEBUG__` tree-shake defines bought 1.6 kB. A dynamic import lands at 251.96 kB, inside the budget, with Sentry in its own chunk. Raising the budget to buy error reporting was the alternative and was declined.

  **Two things that cost paid for.** The lazy import defers the SDK's own `error` and `unhandledrejection` handlers by a round trip, and that window covers hydration — the failure with no other way to be seen, since a module throwing while it evaluates leaves no tree for a boundary to catch. [lib/early-errors.ts](../../../apps/web/src/lib/early-errors.ts) holds those events natively and replays them through `captureException` once the chunk lands, tagged `handled: false` and split between the `onerror` and `onunhandledrejection` mechanisms so a replayed rejection groups where the SDK's own would have. And *when* the listeners install is the whole point, so they go up as a module side effect in [lib/early-errors-install.ts](../../../apps/web/src/lib/early-errors-install.ts), imported first in `client.tsx` — calling it from that file's body would install them only after react-dom had already evaluated.

  **`src/client.tsx` now exists**, overriding Start's generated browser entry (`resolveEntry({ type: 'client entry' })` prefers it). Its body is a copy of Start's default and must be re-checked on a Start upgrade; there is no supported hook for "run this before hydration" short of owning the entry. The browser DSN is a **build argument**, so this is the chunk that needs the account before the first production web image is built. Concretely that means a `VITE_SENTRY_DSN` repository variable alongside `VITE_API_URL` and `VITE_SITE_URL`, wired into the `images` job in `ci.yml` — not into `deploy.sh`, which never sees a build. → [image-pipeline.md](image-pipeline.md)
- **E3 — sourcemaps and releases.** ✅ **Repo side shipped 2026-09-17; needs a `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` repository secret and a `SENTRY_ORG` variable before the upload actually runs.** `build.sourcemap: "hidden"`, `@sentry/vite-plugin` 5.4.0 gated on the token so a local build, a PR check and a fork stay unaffected, release named off `buildCommit` — the same string as the image tag, so an issue names something deployable.

  **`"hidden"` rather than `true`, and the difference was measured.** Both emit the 210 maps the upload needs; `true` also appends `//# sourceMappingURL=` comments, which are counted bytes in the initial JS the budget gates on. `true` landed at 253.59 kB against the 255 kB limit, `"hidden"` at 252.41 kB. Sentry resolves from the upload either way and the maps still ship in the image, so the only loss is devtools resolving them without being asked. Raising the budget to buy error reporting was declined once already; spending 1.2 kB of what is left on a convenience would be the same trade.

  **The token is a BuildKit secret mount, never an ARG.** A build arg is readable through `docker history`, and both packages are anonymously pullable. It reaches the build as `--mount=type=secret` for the one `RUN`, read with `|| true` so an unauthenticated build still succeeds.

  **Both web steps in `ci.yml` carry the secret, and that is not redundancy.** They share `cache-from: type=gha,scope=web`: the build step populates the cache and the push step reuses it, so a token on the push step alone would hit a cached layer built without one and upload nothing while reporting success.

  **`@sentry/cli`'s install script is declined**, tested rather than assumed — the binary it needs arrives through a platform-specific optional dependency (`@sentry/cli-linux-x64` and friends), so `sentry-cli --version` answers with the hook off. pnpm adds the `allowBuilds` entry as a placeholder demanding a decision; `false` is the decision.

  **The first real run failed the upload and reported success anyway — 2026-09-17.** `sentry-cli releases new 2e51a1e` exited 1 in both web steps, the images published, and the job was green. The plugin logs upload failures and lets the build continue by default, which is reasonable for a plugin and wrong here: the image ships, deploys, and serves minified traces while every check says green. That is the exact failure this chunk exists to remove, rebuilt one layer up. An `errorHandler` now rethrows, so a supplied token that cannot upload is a build failure. Verified both ways: no token builds clean with 210 maps, a bad token exits 1.

  **The region was the wrong diagnosis, and the elimination is worth keeping.** A DSN host of `ingest.de.sentry.io` says where a project's *data* lands, not where its API lives — Sentry's control plane is `sentry.io` for every org, and `de.sentry.io` serves only regional data endpoints. Three hypotheses died in order, each ruled out by a status code rather than by argument: not the region (`sentry-cli info` reported `Sentry Server: https://sentry.io` against a single-org account, so there was no second region to be in), not the org slug (a wrong one 404s; this 403s), and not authentication (that 401s). **403 with scope `org:ci` is a permissions answer**: the organization auth token Sentry documents for bundler plugins is not permitted to create a release here, so the fallback is a personal token carrying `project:releases` and `org:read` explicitly.

  `SENTRY_URL` stays wired but defaults to unset. Forcing `https://de.sentry.io/` was harmless only by accident: an `sntrys_` token embeds its own URL and overrides the setting — which is exactly how the mismatch became visible, since sentry-cli warns when it ignores a manual URL. A personal token embeds nothing, so the same default would have sent it to the wrong base and produced a fourth wrong diagnosis.

  **The actual cause, found 2026-09-18: `node:*-slim` ships no CA certificates.** With a working token and the URL plumbing removed, the upload finally reached TLS and died on `SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate`. Verified by running the base image: `/etc/ssl/certs` holds zero PEMs and `ca-certificates` is not installed. **Node bundles its own trust store**, so `pnpm install` reaches the registry and the gap is invisible to every other step in the image; sentry-cli is a Rust binary reading the *system* store, and it is the first thing in this build to need one. The build stage now installs `ca-certificates`, which populates 150 certs and the bundle file.

  Worth keeping as a shape rather than a fact: **four wrong diagnoses preceded it** — region, org slug, token scope, and an empty `SENTRY_URL` the `ARG` exported into the build environment. Each was consistent with the evidence available and each was disproven in under a minute by running something. The one that finally landed came from reading the error text rather than reasoning from the architecture.

  **Superseded — the original regional reasoning:** This org is in the EU — its DSN host is `ingest.de.sentry.io` — while sentry-cli defaults its API base to `sentry.io`, which serves US orgs. An `sntrys_` organization token embeds its region and needs no help; a personal token does not. `SENTRY_URL` is now explicit (default `https://de.sentry.io/`, overridable by a repository variable) so both token types behave the same. Note the `||` rather than `??`: an unset Actions variable interpolates to an empty string, not undefined — the same trap `SENTRY_SAMPLE_RATE` already carries a comment about.

  Original scoping: `build.sourcemap`, the Sentry Vite plugin, release tagging off `BUILD_COMMIT`, which is already threaded end to end: a `compose.prod.yaml` build arg, an `ARG` in `apps/web/Dockerfile`, and the `__BUILD_COMMIT__` define in `vite.config.ts`. Lands after E2 because it only has value once web events exist. The upload half runs *at image build*, so it lands in the same `images` job and wants a `SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN` repository **secret** — the one value in this pipeline that is not a public variable. `BUILD_COMMIT` there is `github.sha` cut to seven, which is also the image tag, so a release name and a deployable tag are the same string. → [image-pipeline.md](image-pipeline.md)

**On needing a Sentry account.** E1a needed none, and the end-to-end scrubbing check does not strictly need one either: a DSN is only a URL the SDK posts envelopes to, so a syntactically valid one aimed at a local endpoint that dumps what arrives shows the raw payload, which is a better scrubbing test than Sentry's rendering of it. **But the browser DSN is a build argument.** It is public by design and gets baked into the bundle, which puts it in the same class as `VITE_API_URL` — fixed at image build time, changed only by rebuilding. The runbook in [hosting.md](hosting.md) already orders DNS before the first build for exactly this reason, and the browser DSN joins it: **it must exist before the first production web image is built**, or client-side reporting is absent until the next rebuild. Since 2026-09-16 that deadline is concrete rather than notional — every push to `main` builds an image, so the variable must be set before the push whose image is meant to be deployed, and a later one is a rebuild rather than a config change. The api DSN has no such constraint; it is an ordinary runtime env var on the box.

**Sequencing:** E1b alone closes the gate in [pre-launch-sweep.md](pre-launch-sweep.md) in the sense that matters — the api is where a silent production failure actually hurts. E2 and E3 should follow before launch but would not, on their own, justify holding it.
